source: Christian, Russek, Griffiths (2026) Resolving Feynman's restaurant problem reveals optimal solutions and human strategies. PNAS
finding: Preregistered one-shot test: people stop with a threshold that falls linearly with the share of trials left, not the curved optimal one.
numbers: N=2,520; one run per person; 4 value distributions x 3 horizons (7,14,28 nights); best model = one shared slope over proportion of nights remaining, free intercepts.
limits: Fixed known values, no real costs. Each person ran the task once, so no learning.
agent_relevance: A cheap linear stop line that tightens as budget runs out is a human-grade rule for S6; code can set it from the remaining budget share.

source: Christian, Russek, Griffiths (2026) Resolving Feynman's restaurant problem reveals optimal solutions and human strategies. PNAS
finding: Thresholds shift with the value distribution in the same order as the optimal policy (Exponential, Power Law above Uniform above Triangular).
numbers: Models forcing equal intercepts fit worse for all pairs except Exponential=Power Law (dBIC -11.1, p=0.023); Triangular=Uniform dBIC 26.4, chi2(3)=84.3, p<0.001.
limits: Intercepts also fall as total nights rise.
agent_relevance: The stop line must be set per problem class, not globally. Class history sets the intercept.

source: Christian, Russek, Griffiths (2026) Resolving Feynman's restaurant problem reveals optimal solutions and human strategies. PNAS
finding: Early over-exploration: people explore more than a linear rule predicts in the first few trials. A decaying bonus fixes the fit.
numbers: Adding the bonus improved fit by dBIC=79.7. Authors suggest one-shot caution as a cause; earlier multi-trial studies did not show it.
limits: Explanation is a hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: An agent may also over-sample early; check early commitment on logs.

source: Christian, Russek, Griffiths (2026) Resolving Feynman's restaurant problem reveals optimal solutions and human strategies. PNAS
finding: Linear thresholds fitted to participants earn nearly as much as the optimal policy.
numbers: Figure 4: optimal linear policies are extraordinarily close to optimal; participant-fitted linear policies and actual scores are nearly as high (exact values in the figure only).
limits: Exact scores not read from text.
agent_relevance: Supports a simple fixed rule instead of solving the full Bellman problem at runtime.

source: Christian, Russek, Griffiths (2026) Resolving Feynman's restaurant problem reveals optimal solutions and human strategies. PNAS
finding: Review of earlier work: Bhatia (cost per option) found risk aversion and subjective search costs explain gaps; Wilson (random end) found fewer samples give lower thresholds and noisier choices; Song and Sang found linear decay.
numbers: Earlier studies had 20 to 200 repeats per person. Sang tested one horizon and one discrete uniform distribution.
limits: Secondhand summary of those papers.
agent_relevance: The linear-threshold finding is replicated across several labs and task variants, with different payoffs.

source: Baumann, Singmann, Gershman, von Helversen (2020) A linear threshold model for optimal stopping behavior. PNAS
finding: Study 1 (10-ticket price search, value payoff): people stop earlier than optimal on average but lose only 6% of optimal earnings.
numbers: Mean 17.1 points per trial (SD 4.2, max 20). Mean stop position 4.7 (SD 2.9) vs optimal 5.2 (SD 2.8). At position 9 accept rate 28% (CI 26-29) vs optimal 50%.
limits: Early positions: accept too soon. From position 7 on: keep searching when they should accept. So not a simple too-early bias.
agent_relevance: Bias depends on position. A stop rule tested on logs should check both early and late errors.

source: Baumann, Singmann, Gershman, von Helversen (2020) A linear threshold model for optimal stopping behavior. PNAS
finding: Linear threshold model (3 parameters) fits as well as a free 9-threshold model; the best-option model fits worse; a cutoff-style model fits terribly.
numbers: Posterior predictive misfit p<.05 for 8% of participants (free thresholds), 35% (best-option model). Cutoff model gamma 0.02 (near random). All participants had positive slopes. No learning over trials, F(1,64)=0.02, p=.88.
limits: One task family in Study 1; later studies tested other environments.
agent_relevance: Rules built for the 1/e secretary problem fit value-based tasks badly. Attempts have check values, so use thresholds, not the 37% rule.

source: Baumann, Singmann, Gershman, von Helversen (2020) A linear threshold model for optimal stopping behavior. PNAS
finding: Background in the paper: in classic rank-only secretary tasks people set the cutoff earlier than the 37% rule; people are heterogeneous but cluster near optimal.
numbers: Cited from refs 1,5,7,8; no numbers in this passage.
quote: people follow a similar strategy but usually set the cutoff ... earlier than the 37% prescribed
limits: Secondhand; original studies (Seale and Rapoport 1997 and others) were not opened.
agent_relevance: Marks the stops-too-early claim as established for rank-only tasks.

source: Costa and Averbeck (2015) Frontal-parietal and limbic-striatal activity underlies information sampling in the best choice problem. Cerebral Cortex
finding: fMRI best-choice task: people draw fewer options than a Bayesian ideal observer and do not scale up enough for longer lists.
numbers: N=32; lists of 8 or 12; rewards $5/$3/$1 for ranks 1-3; 42 trials. Fewer than optimal F(1,31)=16.96, p<.001; interaction with length F(1,31)=24.55; gap significant at 12 (t=4.98) not at 8 (t=1.4, p=.169).
limits: Reward only for top 3 ranks; undersampling is not universal (see van de Wouw, Furl).
agent_relevance: People under-adjust budgets as problems grow. A stop rule should scale the sample budget with problem size.

source: Costa and Averbeck (2015) Frontal-parietal and limbic-striatal activity underlies information sampling in the best choice problem. Cerebral Cortex
finding: A fitted cost-to-sample explains undersampling at the person level.
numbers: Mean cost-to-sample $0.093 (SEM 0.022); improved fit in 16 of 32 people (chi2>6.635); Spearman rho=-0.67 (p=.001) with number sampled.
limits: Helps only half of participants. Later work prefers a biased prior.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: an implicit per-sample cost. For an agent the cost is real tokens and can be set explicitly.

source: van de Wouw, McKay, Furl (2024) Biased expectations about future choice options predict sequential economic decisions. Communications Psychology
finding: Replicated undersampling in a smartphone-price task (pilot baseline), N=47, Cohen d=-2.52 vs the ideal observer.
numbers: 12 options per sequence, top-3 rank reward, Prolific, UK.
limits: Only under top-3 payoff; with full-value payoff the effect shrank or vanished.
agent_relevance: Undersampling replicates but depends on payoff scheme.

source: van de Wouw, McKay, Furl (2024) Biased expectations about future choice options predict sequential economic decisions. Communications Psychology
finding: Task tweaks (ratings phase, squares after choice, timing, payoff) do not change how much people sample.
numbers: Study 1 conditions n=50-51 each; BF01>3 (moderate evidence of no difference) for almost all pairs. Biased Prior model best in all four no-ratings conditions.
limits: Between-subject online sample.
agent_relevance: Human sampling is stubborn: set by expectation, not by instructions or presentation.

source: van de Wouw, McKay, Furl (2024) Biased expectations about future choice options predict sequential economic decisions. Communications Psychology
finding: Undersampling is inconsistent when every choice is paid by its value: the ideal observer itself samples less, so the gap shrinks.
numbers: Study 1 full vs ratings: d=-0.61 vs d=-1.72 against objective-value observer. Study 2 N=151 (new sequences per person): equal to subjective-value observer, undersampled vs objective-value observer.
limits: Pilot full and Study 1 full conflicted; Study 2 was needed.
agent_relevance: Whether a stop rule is too early depends on the payoff. Define the agent's payoff before judging.

source: van de Wouw, McKay, Furl (2024) Biased expectations about future choice options predict sequential economic decisions. Communications Psychology
finding: Best explanation of bias is a pessimistic prior about future options, beating cost-to-sample and a secretary-style cutoff heuristic.
numbers: Study 2 N=151: Biased Prior beat Cut Off (d=-0.87) and Cost to Sample obj (d=-0.45). Study 3 (preregistered): 14 options sampled more than 10 options; undersampling only at 14, slight oversampling at 10.
limits: Cost to Sample contributed more at 14 options. Models were fitted, not tested by intervention.
agent_relevance: A mis-specified expectation of future gain is a failure an agent can share. Estimate the gain of another attempt from logged data, not from the model's feeling.

source: Furl, Averbeck, McKay (2019) Looking for Mr(s) Right: Decision bias can prevent us from finding the most attractive face
finding: Opposite bias: with attractive faces people oversampled, held too-high thresholds, and many sequences ended with no choice.
numbers: Replicated across three studies (abstract); participants sampled more and chose lower-ranked faces than the ideal observer.
limits: Sample sizes not read. Mate-choice domain with self-rated values.
agent_relevance: Overlong search is also a real failure. A stop rule needs a ceiling as well as a floor.

source: Kira, Zylberberg, Shadlen (2025) Incorporation of a cost of deliberation time in perceptual decision making
finding: When time pressure was raised unannounced mid-session, people decided faster and less accurately, and their stopping bounds collapsed more steeply.
numbers: Four human participants; motion strengths 0 to 51.2%; trials cancelled if no decision by a provisional deadline. Bounds approximate an optimal stopping policy but shape varies by person.
limits: N=4 only. Perceptual task, not secretary-style.
agent_relevance: Supports a stop line that tightens with elapsed cost; individual differences are large.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: A Dirichlet-based stopping rule on vote counts cuts samples with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: Up to 3.4x fewer samples at no average accuracy drop; GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4x fewer, <0.2% drop; Vicuna-13B 1.9x fewer; 17 datasets. Maths 3.3x fewer (0.1% drop); commonsense 2.9x (0.2%); code 2.4x (+0.4%).
limits: Votes from one model are not independent (G4); the stop reflects agreement, not truth.
agent_relevance: Direct test of a sequential stop rule at fewer samples; a code-run rule beats a fixed count.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Stop sampling when a window of answers all agree; accuracy almost unchanged.
numbers: Sampling reduced: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%; GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-2 7B; max sample 64 for MATH, 40 otherwise.
limits: Window and max size set by hand.
agent_relevance: A simple window-agrees stop gets most of the savings, in line with a fixed rule such as two agree.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC)
finding: Weighting votes by response confidence stops sooner than count-based adaptive voting.
numbers: Gemma-3-4B on GSM8K: about 70% less cost than plain self-consistency at kept accuracy; example 4 confidence-weighted updates vs 7 uniform (43% fewer). 5 models, 4 datasets, calibration set k=128.
limits: Needs a confidence signal; calibration varies by model and task.
agent_relevance: Confidence can add savings but agreement is only a hint (G4); test at equal tokens.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
finding: More thinking tokens eventually flip correct answers to wrong; the best stop point depends on difficulty.
numbers: R1-32B and s1-32B, AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems). Gain +3.2% per 500 tokens early, negative beyond 12K. Drop 12K to 16K -0.9% (CI -1.4 to -0.4). Flip ratio 3.29 at 12K (CI 2.87-3.82). Stop at 6K: 50% less compute for 6% accuracy loss; indicator early stop keeps 97% of peak accuracy at 60% compute. Easy problems overthink at 2K, hard at 8K.
limits: Only 60 problems; budget forcing with Wait prompts; of 80 negative flips examined 67.5% were genuine overthinking.
agent_relevance: Evidence for per-class thinking budgets and an answer-oscillation signal.

source: Shaikh (2026) Knowing When to Ask for Help: Bayesian Self-Escalation (v1.1)
finding: Escalation mid-generation framed as optimal stopping on a belief of eventual success; real check on a Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to 7B cascade.
numbers: Simulation: 96.0% accuracy escalating 40% of queries vs 91.0% fixed rule, 90.1% always-escalate. Real: streaming policy reaches 75% accuracy with 30.2% less compute than post-hoc routing (14,841 vs 21,273 tokens), +12.7 points over junior alone. Two of three preregistered predictions held.
limits: Tested policy was a constant threshold, not the optimal schedule; single-author preprint; the literal myopic rule over-escalated (62% at token 1).
agent_relevance: A belief-based stop beats post-hoc checking at equal cost, only if the belief is calibrated.

source: Ruan et al. (2026) Doomed from the Start: Early Abort via Recall-Controlled Probe Cascade
finding: Linear probes on hidden states predict agent failure from round 1; a calibrated cascade aborts doomed episodes.
numbers: TextCraft and WebShop; Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3-1.7B. At 90% recall: up to 60.2% fewer tokens (TextCraft), 54.9% (WebShop); at 95% recall 45.0% and 41.5%. Recall within 1 SD of target in all 24 configurations.
limits: Needs model internals; small models.
agent_relevance: Abort gains are large with a recall guarantee; a black-box agent has only behaviour signals, which the paper says do worse.

source: Liu, Qu et al. (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs overshoot or undershoot when to stop; fine-tuning on counterfactual stop/continue pairs improves termination.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for diagnosis, 1,233 training problems; baselines base model and equal-size SFT. Exact gains are in figures, not extracted.
limits: Training-time method; numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Untrained models stop badly, which argues for a code-run stop.

source: Qian (2026) Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal-Dual Certificates
finding: LLM-written exercise policies for Bermudan options do not beat Ridge least-squares Monte Carlo.
numbers: 24 generation attempts, six-pair ablation, frozen holdout; gap scores within 0.002 of Ridge LSMC; on six 1-D puts 99% of the estimated gap is dual-bound looseness; structured memory gave no benefit over score-only memory.
limits: Workshop paper, one lab; the certificate cannot show progress at this scale.
agent_relevance: In a solved stopping task the LLM adds nothing over the classical algorithm; use the algorithm and certify on held-out data (G3).

source: Vatsa and Eiers (2026) Bellman Language Models
finding: Solving the agent's recurring decisions once as an MDP and running the policy as a controller beats having the LLM rederive each move.
numbers: tau2-bench telecom: controller alone solves 79%; Qwen 27B goes 29% to 96% with 93% fewer calls. Unseen-fault set (60 tasks): Qwen alone 67.2% pass1 vs BLM 97.8%. Giving the model the policy as text: 31 to 69 tasks and still 18-23 calls. SymPy: suggested stops followed 6.5%; executed stop cut tokens 36.5% at 40.0% vs 43.3% success (interval -18.3 to +10.0).
limits: Bounded workflows only; little help where writing content is the hard part. One registered token forecast missed.
agent_relevance: Code-executed stops work; suggested stops are ignored. Backs the program decides, the model fills a slot.
